opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few characteristics that matter a lot, and they're somewhat different from what people intuitively expect.

The first is something like the time horizon or the context length of the task. Tasks that can be completed in a few seconds or a few minutes, where you don't need to keep track of a lot of state or a long history of what you've done, seem to be much easier for current AI systems. If you look at how capabilities have progressed, models first got good at short, self-contained things, like answering a single question or writing a small function, and the length of tasks they can reliably complete has been growing over time. So I'd expect jobs that decompose into lots of short, independent subtasks to get automated earlier than jobs that require sustained, coherent work over days or weeks, where you have to plan, revise, and keep a lot of context in your head.

The second is the availability of data and feedback. A lot of what makes AI good at something is whether there's a large amount of training data for it, or whether you can cheaply generate a reliable signal of success. Things like coding or math, where you can check whether the answer is right, are much more amenable to reinforcement learning than tasks where the quality of the outcome is ambiguous, takes a long time to observe, or depends on messy real-world consequences.

Third, and this is the Moravec's paradox point, is whether the task is physical. Sensorimotor skills that humans find trivial, like folding laundry or navigating a cluttered room, have turned out to be very hard for machines, because evolution spent a huge amount of optimization on those abilities and we have relatively little data on them compared to text. So I'd expect a lot of cognitive, remote work to be automated well before physical work, even work we'd think of as low-skill, like plumbing or cleaning.

Then there are non-technical factors that affect deployment rather than capability: regulation, liability, how much people value having a human do it, how costly errors are. Even if AI can technically do a task, adoption could be slow if mistakes are catastrophic or if there are legal barriers.

That said, I want to be careful not to overweight task-by-task analysis. My view is that once you get AI systems that are broadly capable at the level of a human worker, especially at long-horizon agentic work, automation won't happen one narrow task at a time. You'd get something more like a general substitute for labor, and the remaining bottlenecks would mostly be physical capital, robotics, and adoption frictions rather than the specific features of each task.

r001.rationale: The response says sensorimotor tasks such as folding laundry or navigating clutter are hard for machines and predicts cognitive work will be automated well before physical work.

r002.rationale: It says short, self-contained tasks are easier for current AI and that jobs made up of short, independent subtasks are likely to be automated earlier.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss familiarity with a company's internal practices as a factor in automation difficulty.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention outsourcing tasks to contractors or use outsourcing difficulty to predict AI automation difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few dimensions that matter a lot here, and they interact in interesting ways.

The first one is just how much the task depends on things that are hard to get training data for. If you look at where AI has made the fastest progress, it's in domains where there's an enormous amount of digitized data and where the output can be evaluated fairly cheaply, so coding, writing, math, things like that. Tasks where the relevant knowledge is tacit, where it lives in people's heads and isn't written down anywhere, are going to be slower, because you can't just scrape it off the internet. You have to either generate the data through some kind of real-world interaction, or you have to figure out how to transfer skills from other domains.

The second dimension is whether the task involves physical manipulation of the world. I'm fairly pessimistic about robotics relative to cognitive work, just because the data constraints are much worse, the hardware is expensive, and iteration cycles are slow. If you have a software task, you can run millions of trials a day. If you have a robot in a warehouse, you're bottlenecked by physics. So I'd expect purely cognitive tasks to be automated substantially before tasks that require dexterous manipulation in unstructured environments.

The third thing, and I think this is underrated, is the time horizon of the task. Current models are quite good at things that take a human a few minutes or maybe an hour, and they degrade pretty rapidly as the task gets longer. A lot of real jobs aren't a sequence of independent one-hour tasks. They involve maintaining context over weeks or months, dealing with ambiguous goals, noticing when something has gone wrong and recovering from it. Those capabilities seem to be improving, but they're improving along a curve, and tasks that sit far out on that horizon will be automated later.

And then there's a fourth thing that isn't really about the task itself, but about the environment around it. How costly is a mistake? How regulated is the domain? How much does the task require trust or accountability from a specific person? A radiologist reading a scan and a lawyer signing off on a contract are both doing cognitive work that a model might do well, but the institutional friction around replacing them is very different. So you could have a task that's technically automatable but still done by humans for a long time because of liability or because customers simply want a person to be responsible.

If I had to compress it, I'd say the tasks that get automated soonest are short-horizon, digital, verifiable, low-stakes, and data-rich. The ones that take longest are long-horizon, physical, hard to evaluate, high-stakes, and dependent on knowledge that nobody has written down. Most actual jobs are bundles of both kinds of tasks, which is why I expect a lot of the near-term effect to look like partial automation and restructuring of jobs rather than wholesale replacement.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks requiring dexterous physical manipulation in unstructured environments will be automated later than cognitive tasks.

r002.rationale: It says short-horizon tasks are automated sooner, but does not clearly identify narrowly circumscribed tasks as easier to automate.

r003.rationale: It discusses tacit, unwritten knowledge generally, but does not mention familiarity with a company's internal practices.

r004.rationale: It does not connect difficulty outsourcing a task to a contractor with difficulty automating it using AI.

astra-6.text:
I think one important distinction is between how difficult a task is to do and how difficult it is to check whether it’s been done correctly. Those can be quite different. If you can cheaply check the output, you can train on that feedback, and you can have an AI try several approaches and select the one that works. That makes a task more amenable to automation, even if humans find it intellectually difficult.

Programming is a partial example. For some programming tasks, you can run tests and get fairly clear feedback. But deciding what software a customer actually needs, or whether a change will make a large system easier to maintain, is much harder to evaluate. So even within one occupation, I’d expect different tasks to be automated at different times.

Another dimension is how much context the task requires. If everything you need is in a document or a well-defined digital environment, that’s more straightforward than a task that depends on tacit knowledge about an organization, or on interacting with the physical world.

And then there’s the question of reliability. Being able to do something successfully most of the time might be enough for a task where mistakes are cheap and someone reviews the output. It’s much less useful if a rare mistake is very costly, especially if detecting that mistake requires doing the work again.

So I wouldn’t expect automation to proceed neatly from low-skilled jobs to high-skilled jobs. I’d expect it to depend more on whether tasks are well specified, whether success is easy to measure, and how cheaply you can handle failures. And automating a task doesn’t necessarily mean automating the whole job, because the remaining tasks can still require a person.

r001.rationale: The response mentions tasks involving the physical world as less straightforward, but does not identify advanced sensorimotor skills or predict that such tasks will be automated relatively later.

r002.rationale: It says well-specified tasks with measurable success are more amenable to automation, but does not clearly state that narrowly circumscribed tasks are relatively easy to automate.

r003.rationale: It says tasks depending on tacit knowledge about an organization are less straightforward to automate.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss whether a task is difficult to outsource to a contractor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important distinction is between tasks where it's easy to tell whether you've succeeded and tasks where that's much harder. If you can cheaply check the output, you can train on that feedback, and you can also have an AI try several approaches and select the one that works. A programming task with good tests is an example. If you're making a strategic decision whose consequences won't be clear for several years, that feedback is much harder to obtain.

Another dimension is how long the task takes and how reliably each step has to be performed. An AI might be very good at individual steps but still struggle to complete a long project without someone intervening. So I would expect short, well-specified tasks with readily available feedback to be automated earlier than tasks that require sustained judgment in an ambiguous environment.

And then there's the distinction between digital and physical work. For digital tasks, you can often deploy the system using infrastructure that already exists. For physical tasks, you need suitable hardware, and it has to operate reliably in the real world. That adds another set of constraints.

But automating a task isn't the same thing as automating a job. A job is usually a bundle of tasks, and being able to do most of them doesn't necessarily mean you can replace the person. It may instead mean that the person becomes more productive and spends more time on the parts that remain difficult to automate.

r001.rationale: The response says physical work faces hardware and real-world reliability constraints, but does not identify advanced sensorimotor skills as a reason for later automation.

r002.rationale: It predicts that short, well-specified tasks are automated earlier, which communicates that narrowly bounded tasks are easier to automate.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss familiarity with a company's internal practices.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect difficulty outsourcing a task to its difficulty of AI automation.
